title: The Language of the fourth floor walk-up
premise: Rosalind Marchetti, once the conservatory's celebrated piano prodigy, now cleans its corridors under a name nobody connects to the boy on the old recital posters. When Aron Vay, the dying last speaker of a nearly extinct language, asks him to become his final student, Rosalind is forced back into rooms he spent twenty years avoiding. Learning the language becomes a reckoning with his mother, who arranged the family's silence around his abandoned career, and with the question of whether belonging can be inherited or must be chosen. In the end, as Aron dies, Rosalind records the language, plays again for the first time in two decades, and claims both names—Marchetti and prodigy—as his own.
about_author: Petra Marchetti is the pen name of a former conservatory custodian who wrote this novel during night shifts over eleven years. She lives above a shuttered music shop and teaches an endangered dialect to three students she found online.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. We meet him mopping the practice-wing floors at 6 a.m., invisible among students who don't know the posters of 'R. Marchetti, age 12' are him. A visiting professor almost recognizes him; Rosalind deploys his practiced smile. Emotional beat: the comfort and cost of chosen invisibility.

chapters.title: Room 4C
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Sent to clean the fourth-floor walk-up office of Aron Vay, the elderly linguist no department claims, Rosalind finds walls of cassette tapes and a photograph of his mother, young, holding a violin. Aron watches him work and says nothing—yet. Beat: unease, the past surfacing in objects.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Aron's POV. Diagnosed with months to live, Aron decides Rosalind—not a scholar—is the one who should inherit the language, because inheritance needs longing, not credentials. He begins leaving annotated tapes where Rosalind will find them. Beat: quiet scheming, tenderness disguised as accident.

chapters.title: What the Mother Arranged
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A Sunday dinner: his mother deflects every mention of the tapes, revealing in fragments how she ended his career at fifteen to protect the family from his father's debts and her own ambitions. Beat: the family's architecture of silence made visible.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Rosalind finally accepts a lesson; the language has no word for 'prodigy' but twelve for 'belonging.' He stumbles, laughs for the first time in years. Meanwhile Aron hides worsening symptoms. Beat: tentative joy, the risk of wanting something again.

chapters.title: The Poster in the Lobby
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A student photographs him beside his childhood poster; it spreads through the conservatory. Colleagues who ignored him for years now want the story of the fallen genius. His smile stops working. Beat: exposure, shame curdling into anger.

chapters.title: Twelve Words for Belonging
chapters.summary: Aron's POV. Hospitalized, Aron dictates the language's grammar from memory while Rosalind transcribes. Aron confesses he knew Rosalind's mother—she was his student before she chose silence too. Beat: revelation that the family's arrangement echoes a larger pattern of abandonment.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Confronting his mother at the old family house, Rosalind finally asks the question everything was arranged around: why did you let them take it from me? Her answer—fear, love, cowardice braided together—breaks something open rather than closed. Beat: climax of the family arc.

chapters.title: Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Aron's POV, final days. Aron records his last tape: not grammar but a letter, telling Rosalind that languages die when no one dares to be seen speaking them. He dies at dawn with Rosalind reading aloud in the fourth-floor walk-up. Beat: grief fused with purpose.

chapters.title: The Language of the Fourth Floor Walk-Up
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Months later: the archive is donated, a small class meets in Room 4C, and Rosalind sits down at a conservatory piano for the first time in twenty years and plays badly, publicly, unashamed. His mother attends. Beat: resolution—identity claimed, belonging chosen, inheritance accepted.
